rag_semantic_descriptions: A low-and-slow denial of service attack is holding web server connections open for extremely long durations by sending incomplete HTTP headers or extremely slow POST bodies, one byte at a time.
The attacker is deliberately drip-feeding data to the server just fast enough to avoid timeout disconnection, keeping each connection alive for minutes or hours while consuming a server thread.
Unlike volumetric floods, this attack uses almost zero bandwidth — it ties up server resources by occupying connection slots with artificially prolonged, never-completing HTTP requests.
The flow data shows extreme connection longevity with massive deliberate delays between packets, where the client waits until the last millisecond before the server's timeout to send the next byte.
This Slowloris-style attack opens legitimate TCP connections but never finishes sending the HTTP request, keeping the server in a perpetual waiting state for the request to complete.
The average packet sizes are tiny — often just a single byte — because the attacker is fragmenting HTTP headers or POST bodies into the smallest possible pieces to maximize connection duration.
Because the attack uses perfectly valid TCP handshakes and minimal bandwidth, it completely bypasses traditional Layer 3/Layer 4 DDoS mitigation hardware and rate-limiting defenses.
The server's concurrent connection pool is slowly being filled by these lingering half-complete requests, eventually leaving no room for legitimate users to establish new connections.
A Slow POST (R-U-Dead-Yet) variant declares a large Content-Length in the HTTP header but then transmits the actual body at an excruciatingly slow rate, forcing the server to wait.
This could be confused with a legitimate mobile user on a very poor cellular connection, but the pattern of multiple simultaneous slow connections from the same source reveals its malicious intent.
